item.content:encoded:
The war that never ended: Norway, Korea and the UN Command

发布源: Norwegian Institute of International Affairs (NUPI) --Norway | 抓取时间: 2026-11-20

In Norwegian defence circles, South Korea is best known as a supplier of military equipment, including a naval support vessel and artillery systems for the Norwegian Army. Far fewer people know that Norway was one of 22 countries that contributed military support after North Korea invaded South Korea in 1950.

Norway’s contribution was NORMASH, the Norwegian Mobile Army Surgical Hospital. According to Lieutenant General Scott Winter, deputy commander of the United Nations Command, Korea, the hospital treated more than 90,000 patients and performed some 14,000 surgeries.

“It’s certainly not forgotten by the Koreans,” says Winter.

Winter is an officer in the Australian Army and Deputy Commander of the United Nations Command in Korea. He explains that the 1953 armistice was designed to last for weeks or months. The war never formally ended, and 18 of the original 22 nations remain active members of the command.

In conversation with Senior Defence Analyst Per Erik Solli (NUPI), Winter describes how the command is led today. He also covers its access to seven bases in Japan and the maritime operations that enforce UN sanctions against North Korea.

OPTIMISM:In 2017, then-Crown Prince Haakon (partly hidden) and then-Crown Princess Mette-Marit visited Ethiopia with a large business delegation, including Yara, which was set to sign a major agreement to develop a mine in the country's northeastern Afar region.

Ethiopia, 7 November 2017: Dressed in pink, then Crown Princess Mette-Marit shakes hands with President Mulatu Teshome outside the palace in the capital, Addis Ababa. She and then Crown Prince Haakon are on a state visit with a large business delegation, including Yara, which is set to sign a major agreement to develop a mine in the country's north-eastern Afar region. The aim is to extract potassium sulphate.

"Creating jobs for young people in Ethiopia together. Strategic partnership with Yara," writes Kari H. Partapuoli of the Development Fund of Norway on Twitter.

As part of the mining project, Yara has asked the Development Fund to help renovate a disused local vocational school near the proposed mine. The idea is to give local young people vocational training so they can help build and run the mine.

Norad, the Norwegian Agency for Development Cooperation, and the Norwegian Embassy in Ethiopia are enthusiastic about the collaboration, a textbook example of what the aid world calls public-private partnerships (PPPs).

item.content:encoded:
How AI has the potential to reshape democracy, sovereignty and humanity

发布源: Norwegian Institute of International Affairs (NUPI) --Norway | 抓取时间: 2026-11-20

Introduced by NUPI DirectorKari Osland, renowned ethicist and Franciscan friarFather Paolo Benanti– Professor of Moral Philosophy and Ethics of Technology at LUISS and Seattle University, and former AI advisor to Pope Francis – delivers a compelling examination of how artificial intelligence has transformed from a technical debate into a critical instrument of foreign policy and global power.

The first-everNUPI Lecture on International Affairshad the title "AI in International Politics", and was recorded at the University Aula in Oslo 17 November 2026.

Listen to the episode here:

Or listen in your preferred podcast player:

Drawing on real-world cases, from autonomous AI agent attacks to the digital "excommunication" of public officials through privatized tech infrastructure, Benanti warns that we are entering a "software-defined reality". He contrasts emerging Platonic tech-ideologies with Aristotelian democratic principles, posing a fundamental question for our common future: will private technology monopolies dictate societal rules, or can democratic institutions reclaim control? As Winston Churchill famously observed: "First we shape our buildings, thereafter they shape us".

Note: This recording features the introduction by NUPI Director Kari Osland and the complete keynote lecture by Paolo Benanti. We study how political institutions, political processes  and political action shape and are shaped by democracy and rights, economic outcomes and social development.

Rule of law, civil liberties and basic political rights are under threat in countries worldwide.

Our research focuses on the growing pressure against democratic institutions in Africa. We have cooperated closely with African partners for decades and have extensive fieldwork experience.

Our research holds high academic quality and provides concrete input to actors engaged in bilateral work, and to donors and activists navigating the shrinking space for civil society.
